strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and important gap: unsupervised Bayesian model selection and misspecification diagnosis in imaging when only a single noisy measurement is available and priors are implicit (e.g., diffusion, plug-and-play). Existing alternatives (marginal likelihood via nested sampling, harmonic mean estimators, empirical Bayes residuals) are either computationally prohibitive or unreliable, motivating the approach.

The core idea—combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission/measurement splitting—is elegant, well-motivated, and presented clearly. The connection to the marginal likelihood as a limiting case (α→0, likelihood rule) provides a principled framing: the method is a computationally tractable relaxation of the gold standard.

The proposed scoring rules are sensible and complementary: a likelihood-based rule (Eq. 5/8) suited to likelihood misspecification and a posterior-based rule with perceptual embeddings (Eq. 6/9) that is sensitive to prior/OOD misspecification. The theoretical explanation of why Φ2 detects OOD (noise imbalance between y+ and y- creates perceptual discrepancy in hallucinated samples) is convincing and illustrated in Figures 7-10.

Experiments are reasonably broad: a controlled Gaussian toy study analyzing the role of α, K, and dimensionality; kernel model selection where the method substantially outperforms Bayesian/empirical-Bayes residual baselines (86.7% single-shot, 100% few-shot vs. 40-60%); OOD detection on natural images and MRI across blur levels, acceleration factors, and Gaussian/Poisson noise; and Type I error/power tables that roughly respect the nominal 5% level.

Reproducibility is addressed (public code, implementation details in the appendix), and the supplementary material is honest about limitations: slow convergence of the Monte Carlo estimator and growing error with dimension (Figs. 11-13), failure cases of Φ2 at extreme blur or poor α choices (Figs. 15-16), and sensitivity of Φ2 to the choice of perceptual embedding (discussed for MRI).
weaknesses: Theoretical support is thin. There are no formal results on the bias/variance of the fission-based CV estimator, its consistency as K,N grow, or how detection/selection power behaves in high dimensions. The error analysis is confined to a 1D-prior Gaussian toy model where error is shown to grow substantially with dimension m (Fig. 12)—precisely the regime of interest for imaging—so the practical high-dimensional behavior remains empirically observed rather than understood.

The 'fully unsupervised from a single measurement' claim is weakened in the misspecification-testing experiments: the statistical test requires a reference ID dataset (30-60 images) to calibrate the 95th-percentile threshold of Φ2. Model selection against a known reference model is one thing; calibrated OOD testing without any reference data is not demonstrated.

The hyperparameter α materially affects results (Figs. 1, 14, 15 show large changes in detection power and error rates across α), but there is no principled procedure for choosing it; different experiments use α = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 apparently by hand. A methodology that requires case-by-case tuning of a central knob limits ease of adoption.

Baseline comparisons are limited. The only quantitative comparison is against the residual method [55] in the kernel-selection experiment; for OOD detection, the recent unsupervised diffusion-based OOD method [48]—which the paper itself cites—is not compared against, making it hard to judge the incremental value of the new machinery for that task.

The posterior-based rule Φ2 is heuristic rather than a proper scoring rule, and its behavior depends strongly on the embedding (LPIPS fails on some cases; DINOv2 recovers 100% accuracy on brain images). The framework's performance is thus partly contingent on embedding choices that are not well characterized, and the paper's failure modes (e.g., Φ2 favoring a hallucinating model in Fig. 20a) are acknowledged but not resolved.

Some evaluations rest on very small samples (e.g., 15 selection experiments in Table 5; 30 test images in Table 2), so accuracy/power estimates carry substantial uncertainty; no confidence intervals or repeated trials are reported for the main tables.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underserved problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification testing for Bayesian imaging inverse problems from a single noisy measurement, which is a real bottleneck for deploying data-driven priors in scientific imaging.

The core idea of combining data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) with Bayesian cross-validation is elegant and natural, and the connection to posterior predictive checks and the marginal likelihood (Section 3.3, Eqs. 10-11) is clearly articulated, positioning the method as a computationally tractable relaxation of evidence computation.

The methodology is sampler-agnostic and demonstrated with both plug-and-play Langevin (SK-ROCK) and diffusion-based (DiffPIR) samplers, plus extensions to Poisson noise, supporting the generality claim.

The supplementary material is thorough: analytical derivations for the Gaussian case, ablations over alpha and K, negative-result discussions (e.g., failure cases in Fig. 16, effect of blur strength on detection power), and implementation details.
Empirical results are respectable: 86.7% single-shot kernel selection accuracy versus 40-60% for the residual-based baselines, and reasonable Type I error/power calibration in the OOD experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility statement is broken: the code URL, model links, and dataset links are literally blank in the manuscript ('available at' followed by nothing). For a paper whose main claims are entirely empirical, this is a serious deficiency for verification at review time.

No theoretical analysis of the proposed estimators. The paper provides no bias/variance analysis of Phi-hat for the actual estimators used (Eqs. 8-9), only an empirical Gaussian toy study. Notably, Phi1 averages log-likelihoods while the logarithmic score applies log to an average; the Jensen gap between these is acknowledged but never quantified, and its magnitude relative to model discrimination gaps in high dimensions (Fig. 12 shows relative error growing with m) is not established.

The mechanism underlying the posterior-based rule Phi2 is presented only heuristically ('noise imbalance creates a noticeable perceptual discrepancy'). It is unclear whether Phi2 measures model misspecification or is confounded by image content: LPIPS-embedding distances between posterior samples may simply track whether the prior can represent the image, which overlaps with, but is not identical to, prior misspecification. The MRI results (Phi2 underperforming Phi1 on knee images, requiring a switch to DINOv2 embeddings to reach 100%) underscore that the method's success depends on embedding choices that are not principled.

Baselines are thin. The only quantitative comparisons are against the Bayesian/empirical-Bayesian residual methods of [55] on a 3-image kernel-selection task with 5 candidate kernels. No comparison against the diffusion-based unsupervised OOD method cited as [48], which is the closest related work; the paper claims novelty ('no existing methods can diagnose OOD based on a single measurement') without empirically substantiating the advantage over that prior work.

Several methodological choices are ad hoc: alpha is hand-tuned per experiment (0.5, 0.1, 0.25 with a different rationale in each), the statistical test is a raw 95th-percentile threshold on a reference dataset, and no guidance is given on how to set K, N, or alpha in a new application. The reported excellent results thus partly reflect careful per-experiment tuning that practitioners cannot easily replicate.

Experimental scope is narrow relative to the framing: only Gaussian/Poisson deblurring and single-coil MRI, with small test sets (e.g., 15 single-shot selection trials, 30-90 test images for OOD). The claimed generality ('compatible with any Bayesian imaging sampler', 'general methodology') is not stress-tested on, e.g., severely ill-posed or nonlinear operators where the likelihood-based rule is acknowledged to have poor discrimination.

There is a tension in the story: the paper notes that alpha -> 0 recovers the marginal likelihood (the gold standard) but that this limit requires more Monte Carlo samples, and Fig. 1 shows discrimination degrading as alpha grows. Since the practical setting used for diffusion experiments is alpha = 0.1-0.25 with K = 4-10 noise realizations and N = 10-20 posterior samples per realization (explicitly under-converged per Fig. 18), the link between the framework's motivating theory and the operating regime actually used is weak, and it is not shown whether a simpler alternative (e.g., direct sample-based prior/likelihood sanity checks) would do comparably.
